generation.hypothesis: Introducing a specific alloying element, such as ZrC, can improve the resistance to thermally induced toughness loss in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) by enhancing the stability of the passive film and reducing the dissolution rate.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy (HEA) in its initial, unalloyed state
generation.intervention: Introduction of a specific alloying element, such as ZrC
generation.conditions: High-temperature annealing conditions, similar to those used in demanding engineering applications
generation.structural_mediator: Stability of the passive film and reduction of the dissolution rate
generation.mechanism: Derived from materials-science principles, based on the effect of alloying elements on the stability of the passive film and the dissolution rate, as well as the role of crystal defects and dislocation motion in determining the mechanical properties of HEAs.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved resistance to thermally induced toughness loss, resulting in enhanced mechanical properties and performance in demanding engineering applications.
generation.baseline: Unalloyed high-entropy alloy (HEA) without the introduction of a specific alloying element
generation.boundary: High-temperature annealing conditions, specific alloy composition, and application context
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism by which the introduction of a specific alloying element improves the resistance to thermally induced toughness loss is not fully understood and requires further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: High-temperature annealing experiment with and without the introduction of a specific alloying element, such as ZrC, to evaluate the effect on the resistance to thermally induced toughness loss.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the introduction of a specific alloying element does not result in improved resistance to thermally induced toughness loss, the hypothesis is falsified.

Consequently, the addition of ZrC to the FeCoCrNiMn high-entropy alloy coating holds promise for applications in corrosion resistance, particularly in oceanic environments.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs), which were originally developed as concentrated solid solutions of multiple principal elements in equal, or near equal, atomic ratios, have drawn progressively increasing attention over the past decade. Unlike single principal-element alloys, their complex alloy compositions and elemental distribution, together with crystal lattice distortion induced by atomic-size mismatch (depending upon relative atomic sizes), can have a significant effect on the activity of their crystal defects and hence mechanical properties. Although HEAs were initially designed to benefit from single-phase stabilization,, single-phase HEAs are actually not that common, and of those that do exist, only a few display excellent damage-tolerance in the form of combinations of high strength, ductility, and toughness. The well-studied equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi Cantor alloy and its derivatives, in particular the CrCoNi alloy, show exceptional damage-tolerance which progressively improves at cryogenic temperatures, although even these alloys do not have yield (as opposed to ultimate tensile) strengths that are comparable to some advanced steels.
